Biblical Infallibility
BIB-li-kuhl in-FAL-uh-BIL-uh-tee
n. phrase (bibliology)
From Latin in (not) + fallere (to deceive, to fail) + -ibilis (capable of). Biblical infallibility is the doctrine that Scripture cannot fail its declared purposes—it does not mislead, does not deceive, and will always accomplish what God intends through it. Often paired with inerrancy (no factual errors) though technically distinct from it.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Biblical infallibility is the teaching that the Scriptures, as the Word of the God who cannot lie, are incapable of failing their purpose or leading God's people into error. Christ Himself established the floor: “the Scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35)—an offhand comment that assumes the inviolability of Scripture as a fixed axiom. Peter teaches that no prophecy of Scripture came from the will of man, but that men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Pet 1:21). Because the Author is God, the Book partakes of God's own infallibility. Numbers 23:19 grounds it in the divine character: “God is not a man, that He should lie, nor a son of man, that He should repent.” Isaiah 55:11 extends it to purpose: “so shall My word be that goes forth from My mouth; it shall not return to Me void, but it shall accomplish what I please.” Infallibility differs from inerrancy in emphasis. Inerrancy focuses on factual accuracy—the Bible contains no falsehoods. Infallibility focuses on purposive reliability—the Bible will not fail to lead those who receive it in faith to God's intended end. In practice, Reformed confessionalism affirms both: a Scripture that could err would also fail, and a Scripture that could fail would deceive—both are impossible given the nature of the God who inspired it. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (1.4, 1.5) affirms Scripture's authority as grounded in God Himself, whose truth cannot fail.

Webster 1828 Definition

The doctrine that Scripture, authored by the God who cannot lie, cannot fail in its declared purposes—it will not mislead, will not deceive, and will always accomplish what God intends through it.

expand to see more

BIBLICAL INFALLIBILITY, n. phrase. The doctrine that Scripture is incapable of leading the faithful astray, of failing its stated purposes, or of deceiving in matters of faith and life—grounded in the nature of God as the Author who cannot lie.

Technically distinguished from inerrancy: inerrancy concerns accuracy (no false statements); infallibility concerns reliability (will not fail its purpose). Reformed confessionalism affirms both as inseparably bound: the God who cannot lie produces a Book that neither errs nor fails.

Christ's appeal to the inviolability of Scripture in John 10:35 is foundational: treating the permanence of Scripture as so self-evident it requires no argument is itself a testimony to the church's pre-critical assumption of Scripture's infallibility.

Isa 55:11 frames infallibility eschatologically: the Word always accomplishes God's intent. It is not merely accurate as a record of the past; it is efficacious as an instrument of God's purposes in the present.

The practical implication: the believer may stake their soul on Scripture. It will not mislead on the way of salvation, will not leave them without light in darkness, and will not return empty to God.

Key Scripture

John 10:35 — "If He called them 'gods,' to whom the word of God came — and the Scripture cannot be broken —"

2 Peter 1:21 — "For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man — but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit."

Numbers 23:19 — "God is not a man, that He should lie, nor a son of man, that He should repent. Has He said, and will He not do? Or has He spoken, and will He not make it good?"

Isaiah 55:11 — "so shall My word be that goes forth from My mouth; it shall not return to Me void, but it shall accomplish what I please, and it shall prosper in the thing for which I sent it."

Modern Corruption

Neo-orthodox and progressive evangelicals since the 20th century have attempted to retain ‘infallibility’ as a label while denying inerrancy—claiming Scripture is infallible in matters of faith and practice but may err in history and science. This is a redefinition that guts both terms.

expand to see more

The neo-orthodox corruption appeared with Karl Barth and was systematized by the post-Barth evangelical left: Scripture is the vehicle through which the Word of God encounters the soul, but the vehicle itself may contain historical, scientific, or even theological inaccuracies. “Infallibility” is retained as a pious label but redefined to mean infallibility in salvific intent, not in factual content. This is not a refinement but a capitulation: a Scripture that may contain false statements in history is also a Scripture that may mislead in doctrine, since the two are inseparable in revelation. A God who inspired a factually errant Bible could just as well have inspired a doctrinally errant one; the same character of truthfulness is required for both.

The practical effect is that the believing community, not Scripture itself, becomes the arbiter of where Scripture speaks reliably. Progressive evangelicalism moves this direction by treating biblical sexuality passages as culturally conditioned, treating creation narratives as mythological rather than historical, and treating the Pauline household codes as time-bound rather than creational. In each case, infallibility is nominally claimed and practically dissolved. The Reformed answer is that if Scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35), this applies to all of it, not merely to the portions modern sensibility finds congenial.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin in-fallere (cannot deceive or fail), grounded in the divine character of God who cannot lie, producing a Word that will accomplish every purpose for which He sent it.

expand to see more

Latin in + fallere — not to fail, not to deceive; the root describes the impossibility of failure given the character of the Author.

John 10:35 — ‘the Scripture cannot be broken’; Christ's offhand axiom treats infallibility as a settled premise, not a doctrine requiring defense.

Isa 55:11 — the Word will not return void; purposive infallibility—God's Word always accomplishes what He sends it to do.

Num 23:19 — God cannot lie; divine truthfulness is the ontological ground of scriptural infallibility.

2 Pet 1:21 — men spoke from God as carried by the Spirit; the mode of inspiration guarantees the infallibility of the product.

Usage

"Biblical infallibility means the believer can stake their soul on Scripture: it will not mislead on the way of salvation, will not leave them in permanent darkness on essential matters, will not fail to accomplish God's purpose in their life."

"Infallibility and inerrancy belong together: a Scripture that errs in history is capable of erring in doctrine, and a doctrine-erring Scripture is a failing Scripture—which infallibility explicitly denies."

"The Reformed confessions affirm both by grounding them in God's character: the Bible is reliable because God is reliable, and what God breathes out (2 Tim 3:16) partakes of His own impossibility of deception."
